Article Title: Children's Hospital Los Angeles raises record $1.35 billion in fundraising campaign supported by Jimmy Kimmel and Jamie Lee Curtis
Article Text:
Getty Images

From one horseback visit to a global name

A night that started with a patient’s family

Two longtime supporters honoured

Getty Images

Children’s Hospital Los Angeles (CHLA) has raised a record $1.35 billion through its 125th Anniversary Campaign, with the support of thousands of donors, including honorary campaign chairs Jimmy Kimmel Jamie Lee Curtis , Sugar Ray Leonard and Chuck Lorre. This is the largest fundraising effort in CHLA’s history. The funds will help advance paediatric care, medical research and education for children and families.In 1901, Children’s Hospital Los Angeles opened in a small house dedicated to children, and its first year brought 14 patients. One physician led the work and travelled on horseback to reach young patients across the region. Today, the hospital oversees more than 750,000 patient visits a year, drawing families from across the United States and more than 90 countries. The change came in steps. In 1930, its physicians performed the first paediatric heart surgery on the West Coast. In 1978, it built a comprehensive paediatric cancer programme, and it now runs one of the first and largest CAR T-cell therapy programmes in the country. By 1993, it had joined early gene therapy research for a rare inherited immune disorder. Its training programmes for paediatricians, nurses and researchers are among the largest in the country.Paul S. Viviano, the hospital’s president and CEO, puts it simply: the team has “continually pushed the boundaries of care”.The fundraising campaign was held at The Event Deck at L.A. LIVE, bringing together philanthropists, community leaders, celebrities, patients and supporters to celebrate the historic achievement. Gina Rodriguez, the Golden Globe-winning actress who hosted the evening, opened the event by talking about her own experience. Her daughter, Lucy, was treated at the hospital’s Neurological Institute. “Today Lucy is totally fine and everyone we encountered during our time at CHLA was absolutely amazing,” Rodriguez said. “I’m thrilled to show my appreciation by welcoming you here tonight to honour the amazing supporters of the hospital and enjoy some outstanding entertainment.”The evening also featured Grammy winner Michael Bublé, who sang hits including “Fly Me to the Moon” and “Feeling Good”.Nikki DeLoach and Jeffrey Worthe co-chaired the campaign. Both have long served the hospital. The honorary campaign chairs include Jimmy Kimmel, Sugar Ray Leonard, Chuck Lorre and Jamie Lee Curtis.Paul S. Viviano, the hospital’s president and chief executive, credited thousands of donors, corporate partners, foundations, families and staff members. He said the money would help the hospital stay at the forefront of paediatric medicine and accelerate scientific discoveries. “Thanks to the remarkable generosity of our supporters, CHLA will continue to be at the forefront of paediatric medicine, accelerate scientific discoveries and ensure children have access to world-class care for generations to come. ”The event also recognised the campaign’s longtime supporters: radio personality and host Ellen K, and Kourtney and Justin Turner. They were honoured with The Courage to Care Award. Ellen K’s ties to the hospital began when her son, Calvin, received emergency care after a serious injury. Since then, she has helped raise more than $4 million through KOST 103.5’s annual Giving Tuesday broadcast. “As a forever-grateful mom and as a member of the Board of Trustees, I will continue showing up for CHLA in every way I can,” she said.Kourtney and Justin Turner were recognised for more than a decade of volunteering, fundraising and advocacy. Through the Justin Turner Foundation, they have supported children facing serious illnesses. Justin Turner recalled that when he played for the Dodgers, the hospital was almost on his way home from the stadium. “It has been a gift to get involved with this hospital. When I was with the Dodgers, CHLA was literally on my way home from the stadium. I visited as much as I could, and so did Kourtney. Children’s Hospital Los Angeles is one of the most amazing institutions in our city.”Drew Barrymore, Jamie Lee Curtis, Pau Gasol, Heidi Klum, Natalie Portman, the LA Kings, Panda Express, The Walt Disney Company, Chuck Lorre, Bernadette and Sugar Ray Leonard, and AEG were among the past recipients of the Courage to Care Award.Meanwhile, Olympian Jordan Chiles presented a Mission Moment highlighting the Jackie and Gene Autry Orthopedic Center, which treats thousands of children with bone and joint conditions every year. The centre runs one of the largest paediatric spine and neuromuscular programmes in the country and offers services in hip preservation, sports medicine, and hand and upper extremity care.The night ended with Bublé performing some of his most beloved hits, including ‘You’re Nobody Till Somebody Loves You’, ‘Fly Me to the Moon’, ‘Such A Night’, ‘Haven’t Met You Yet’, ‘Feeling Good’ and ‘Song For You’.“It’s really special to be here tonight and perform for Children’s Hospital Los Angeles, which means so much to my family. Our family knows firsthand how much the people here care. We’ll always be grateful for the way they were there for us and for everything they do for kids and families,” Bublé said.
Article Summary: This is the largest fundraising effort in CHLA’s history. The funds will help advance paediatric care, medical research and education for children and families. The fundraising campaign was held at The Event Deck at L.A. LIVE, bringing together philanthropists, community leaders, celebrities, patients and supporters to celebrate the historic achievement.

Article Title: After more than 20 years of Halloween builds, a Milwaukee couple transformed the fronts of three neighbouring homes into a Hogwarts-inspired attraction in 2026, while donations for homeless youth pass
Article Text:
Photo credit: Screenshot from TMJ4 News via YouTube

A Hogwarts across three homes

Two decades of building

A tradition of giving

Photo credit: Screenshot from TMJ4 News via YouTube

Why the cause matters

A display with a deadline

In Milwaukee’s Bay View neighborhood, Halloween has become something much larger than a front-porch decoration contest. A&J’s Halloween House, created by Andy Reid and Jamie Beauchamp, has spent more than two decades turning residential properties into elaborate seasonal worlds, and its 2026 Harry Potter-inspired display is the biggest version yet. According to TMJ4 and Hoodline, the attraction now stretches across three neighboring homes and has helped raise more than $100,000 for Pathfinders, a nonprofit supporting homeless and runaway youth.The display, located at 2943 S. Clement Ave., transforms the block into a miniature wizarding world. Visitors can find Hagrid’s hut, the Sorting Hat, Gringotts, the Great Hall, Dobby, a dragon, a giant spider, a troll and figures of Harry Potter and Lord Voldemort, all built into a sprawling neighborhood-scale set.This year’s display is not limited to one front yard. It spans three neighboring homes, giving the creators enough space to build a more immersive version of Hogwarts than they have attempted before. The result includes a Gringotts facade, Hagrid’s hut and a Hogwarts Express train car that visitors can climb into, as per the reports.Inside the train car, a video monitor makes it appear as though Milwaukee is rolling past outside the window, with dementors hovering in the sky.It is a small detail, but it captures the spirit of the display: the creators are not simply arranging decorations, they are building a world that rewards visitors who look closely.The attraction also includes moving portraits featuring Severus Snape, Albus Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall, along with an unexpected cameo by Dolly Parton. Jack-o’-lantern-themed Gringotts goblins add another layer of Halloween mischief to the wizarding theme, suggested the reports.Co-creator Andy Reid told TMJ4 that this year required “a crazy amount” of engineering, design and building. After more than 20 years of Halloween projects, he and Beauchamp have learned how to turn a neighborhood block into a destination.Reid and Beauchamp have been creating Halloween displays together for more than two decades. Their work began with Reid’s memories of his mother’s elaborate Halloween decorations, and it has grown into an annual tradition that draws visitors from across Milwaukee and beyond.The Harry Potter theme is the largest display they have created so far, but it follows a long list of ambitious concepts. Previous years have included Scooby-Doo, Wheel of MisFortune, Ancient Aliens, Ghostbusters, Beetlejuice and a scary circus, according to TMJ4.The 2025 Scooby-Doo display was especially elaborate, featuring a two-story haunted mansion facade, a Mystery Machine replica and a pirate ship built with lumber donated by local supplier Bliffert Lumber. Earlier themes included a Wheel of Fortune scene in 2022 and an Ancient Aliens display with UFOs and pyramids in 2024.The creators store their materials in a garage between seasons, and some pieces are later donated to local schools. They do not disclose the cost of building each display, saying that the expense is their personal donation so that visitor contributions can go directly to the charity.A&J’s Halloween House has partnered with Pathfinders for 11 official years. The nonprofit provides housing support, shelter for runaway and homeless youth, anti-sexual violence services and other assistance to young people in Milwaukee.Last year marked a milestone for the partnership. After a decade of fundraising, the display had raised $102,000 for Pathfinders, according to TMJ4. That total has since been surpassed, making the 2026 season another important chapter in the effort.The fundraising goal was set deliberately. Reid and Beauchamp had raised $84,000 by the end of the 2025 season and hoped to collect $16,000 more to reach $100,000. The milestone has now been passed, according to TMJ4’s reporting.Donations can be made at multiple collection points around the display. The setup makes it easy for visitors to contribute while enjoying the attraction, turning a neighborhood Halloween tradition into a practical source of support for young people in crisis.Pathfinders was founded in 1970 by members of Plymouth Church, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee faculty and local residents as a shelter for runaway youth. Today, the organization operates Milwaukee’s only dedicated youth street outreach team and serves about 5,000 young people each year, according to Pathfinders.The need is significant. A May 2025 report by the Wisconsin Policy Forum, cited by the Wisconsin Justice Initiative, found that Wisconsin K-12 student homelessness reached a record 20,195 students in the 2023-2024 school year. Milwaukee accounted for more than a quarter of the state’s homeless students and 40.7 percent of its unaccompanied homeless youth.Against that backdrop, A&J’s Halloween House does more than entertain. It gives neighbors a reason to gather, gives children a memorable experience and channels community generosity toward an organization that helps young people find safety and stability.The Hogwarts-inspired attraction remains up through October, but it comes down immediately after Halloween. That short window adds urgency for visitors who want to see it before the creators begin dismantling another year of work.Reid has said that the team does not want people to expect an even bigger display next year, though he leaves open the possibility that they may make it better in other ways. After more than 20 years of building, the challenge is no longer simply scale. It is finding new ways to surprise a community that has come to expect something extraordinary.For now, the three-home Hogwarts display stands as both a neighborhood spectacle and a fundraising engine. It proves that Halloween can be more than costumes and candy, and that a front yard can become a place where creativity, community and compassion come together.
Article Summary: A&J’s Halloween House has spent more than two decades turning residential properties into elaborate seasonal worlds. The 2026 Harry Potter-inspired display is the biggest version yet. The attraction has helped raise more than $100,000 for Pathfinders, a nonprofit supporting homeless and runaway youth.

Article Title: Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53 giant burrowing frogs into the forests where they
Article Text:
Native to south-eastern Australia, these elusive frogs inhabit forests stretching across New South Wales and Victoria.

From fire survivors to conservation success

An elusive species facing multiple threats

Returning home with a scientific purpose

Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53 giant burrowing frogs into the forests where they were foundThe aftermath of a devastating wildfire can leave more than scorched trees and damaged landscapes. Sometimes, it reveals unexpected survivors. In Australia's East Gippsland region, a discovery made among the remains of the catastrophic 2019–2020 Black Summer bushfires has grown into an extraordinary conservation success. Nearly six years after the fires devastated their habitat, 53 critically endangered Southern Giant Burrowing Frogs have returned to the forests, following years of specialist care and a pioneering captive-breeding programme.According to ABC News, the frogs were originally discovered as approximately 160 tadpoles in small pockets of water after the fires destroyed extensive areas of their natural habitat. Despite the widespread destruction, the surviving tadpoles offered scientists an opportunity to protect a species whose numbers were already under pressure.Herpetologist Matt Clancy of Snowline Ecology took the rescued tadpoles to Healesville Sanctuary in 2021.According to reports, Zoos Victoria's Melbourne Zoo and Healesville Sanctuary amphibian goalkeepers adapted to captivity.The first Southern Giant Burrowing Frog captive breeding occurred in 2025, marking another program milestone. Zoos Victoria described the achievement as a world first, marking an important step towards securing the species' future.Despite its name, the Southern Giant Burrowing Frog is a relatively compact amphibian, with adults roughly the size of a cricket ball and has large eyes, muscular limbs, and a bright yellow body.According to Zoos Victoria, the species is native to south-eastern Australia, with its range extending from areas south of Kangaroo Valley in New South Wales through Victoria to Walhalla in central Gippsland.However, estimating its remaining population is particularly challenging. As ABC News reported, these frogs spend much of their lives underground, emerging primarily to breed following heavy rainfall. Males can sometimes be detected calling for just one night before disappearing underground for years.Habitat destruction, prolonged drought, bushfires and chytridiomycosis, a widespread amphibian disease, have all contributed to declining populations. Victoria currently has fewer than five known breeding sites.The release of 53 frogs is not simply a return to their original habitat. It also gives researchers an opportunity to understand more about their movements, survival and breeding behaviour.Zoos Victoria explained that each released frog received a microchip or passive integrated transponder (PIT) tag. These identifiers will allow researchers to recognise individual animals during future population surveys and establish how far they have travelled from their release locations.Song meters have also been installed throughout the forest to record the frogs' distinctive calls and help field teams locate potential breeding sites.The conservation partnership between Zoos Victoria and Snowline Ecology has therefore moved into a crucial new phase. With the frogs now sexually mature and their genetics secured for future generations, researchers hope they will contribute to rebuilding wild populations, the ABC News report states. Also, it is reported that the Wildlife and Habitat Bushfire Recovery Program of Australia funded the project.Images Courtesy: Zoos Victoria
Article Summary: Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53 giant burrowing frogs into the forests where they were found. The Southern Giant Burrowing Frog is native to south-eastern Australia, with its range extending from areas south of Kangaroo Valley in New South Wales through Victoria.

Article Title: In 1944, a German U-boat sank the SS Cornwallis off Maine, killing 43 sailors; 82 years later, a dive team ended a seven-year search by locating the wreck almost 400 feet underwater in July 2026
Article Text:
AI representative Image

What happened to the SS Cornwallis in 1944?

German U-boat sank the SS Cornwallis off Maine, killing 43 sailors

How did the dive team finally locate the wreck after seven years?

Location of the sinking of SS Cornwallis

What makes the discovery of the SS Cornwallis historically significant?

SS COrnwallis (Image courtesy- Nomad Exploration team - official)

In a world where miles feel like inches, almost everybody is connected to each other. The whole world has become one village; yet the ocean floor still remains one of the most mysterious places for scientists. You’d be surprised to know that scientists now know more about outer space than they do about the ocean floor.The ocean has a way of holding on to secrets, sometimes for decades and even centuries. Beneath its vast surface lie the remains of ships that once carried people, cargo and stories, many of which were never meant to be forgotten. One such story dates back to the Second World War, when a German submarine torpedoed a Canadian merchant ship off the coast of Maine, sending it beneath the waves in a matter of minutes.On December 3, 1944, the SS Cornwallis was travelling along the Maine coast when it was struck by a torpedo fired by German submarine U-1230. Of the 48 people aboard, only five survived. For more than 80 years, the ship's final resting place remained a mystery. However, in July 2026, a team of divers finally located the wreck, nearly 400 feet beneath the surface, bringing a decades-old search to an end.Imagine being aboard a ship, sailing across the Atlantic, with the journey almost nearing its end.The crew had no reason to believe that this ordinary voyage would turn into a tragedy. The SS Cornwallis had left Barbados on November 20, 1944, carrying bags of sugar and barrels of molasses, and was heading towards Saint John, New Brunswick. However, as the ship travelled along the New England coast on December 3, it encountered a German submarine, U-1230.Commanded by Hans Hilbig, the submarine fired a torpedo that struck the forward section of the Cornwallis. The impact was devastating, and the ship began sinking by the bow, disappearing beneath the water in less than 10 minutes.As per the Canadian Virtual War Memorial, out of the 48 people aboard, six managed to escape in a lifeboat. Although they were eventually rescued by a fishing boat, one of them died from hypothermia. In the devastating attack, only five survived, while 43 people lost their lives.Finding a shipwreck that has remained lost for more than eight decades is no easy task, especially when it lies hundreds of feet beneath the ocean. For the Nomad Exploration Team, the search for the SS Cornwallis began in 2019 and involved years of research, multiple expeditions and hours spent studying historical records.The team first narrowed down three possible locations using historical records, including the coordinates from the ship's distress call, reports of debris spotted from the air and the location where fishermen had rescued the survivors. They also studied historical weather conditions, tide charts and the ship's blueprints to understand where it might have gone down. Over five expeditions, the divers scanned more than 50 square miles of the ocean floor.However, the discovery almost slipped through their hands. On July 11, 2026, during their fifth search expedition, the team was scanning the final stretch of a search grid when the shipwreck appeared on their sonar. They had actually passed close to the wreck once before without recognising it. This time, a more sophisticated side-scan sonar device helped them capture a clearer image of the vessel.But a sonar image alone was not enough to establish its identity. The divers eventually descended nearly 400 feet beneath the surface to examine the wreck themselves. By comparing the remains with the original blueprints of the SS Cornwallis, they confirmed that they had finally found the missing ship.The discovery is particularly significant because the sinking of the SS Cornwallis was connected to a wider German operation along the American coast. Just four days before the attack, German submarine U-1230 had landed two German spies, Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh, in Maine. The discovery of the wreck therefore brings renewed attention to an important chapter of the Second World War and helps researchers understand the maritime history of the region.The ocean floor is perhaps one of the few places where history can remain untouched for generations, waiting to be discovered. The finding of the SS Cornwallis is not simply about locating a sunken ship; it is also about bringing back a story that had remained beneath the waves for more than eight decades. While the wreck may have finally been found, the 43 people who lost their lives remain an important part of its history. Sometimes, discovering the past is also a way of ensuring that it is not forgotten.
Article Summary: German U-boat sank the SS Cornwallis off Maine, killing 43 sailors in 1944. For more than 80 years, the ship's final resting place remained a mystery. In July 2026, a team of divers finally located the wreck, nearly 400 feet beneath the surface, bringing a decades-old search to an end. The discovery is particularly significant because the sinking was connected to a wider German operation along the American coast.

Article Title: In 2019, oil was found seeping from a California railyard into the Sacramento River; six years later, cleanup had removed 75,000 gallons of oil and 100,000 tons of contaminated soil.
Article Text:
Image Courtesy- EPA official website

How did authorities clean up the decades-old oil contamination?

Image Courtesy- EPA official website

What does the cleanup mean for the Sacramento River and its wildlife?

(EPA Official website )

We measure pollution by what we can see: smoke rising from factories, plastic floating in rivers, or oil spreading across the surface of water. But some of the most persistent environmental damage happens quietly, beneath the ground, sometimes for generations. Among those hidden places, A railway yard may seem like an unlikely place for an environmental crisis, but what lies beneath the ground can sometimes be more dangerous than what meets the eye. And that's exactly what happened in California, US.In Dunsmuir, California, oil from an old locomotive-fuelling facility had been leaking into the surrounding soil and the Sacramento River for decades. It was not until in 2019, that the scale of the contamination came forward only when authorities began investigating the seepage.The investigation revealed that the problem was much older than initially understood. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the contamination could be traced back to the early 1900s, when leaking tanks and equipment were used to fuel locomotives at the railyard. Over the years, oil accumulated in the surrounding soil and continued to seep towards the river.In 2021, the EPA began working with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board and Union Pacific Railroad to address the source of the contamination.The cleanup involved removing oil-contaminated soil, dealing with the seepage along the riverbank and restoring the affected shoreline.The cleanup was a multi-year operation that involved removing contaminated soil and oil from the railyard and rebuilding the affected riverbank. Crews first excavated the oil-contaminated soil and removed portions of an existing retaining wall along the Sacramento River. They then brought in clean soil and installed a special barrier fill designed to prevent any remaining oil from seeping into the river.The work also involved restoring around 1,400 feet of the affected shoreline, improving the river's capacity and creating additional habitat for wildlife. By November 2025, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had completed its oversight of the major removal work, which had taken out approximately 75,000 gallons of oil and 100,000 tons of contaminated soil.The restoration work was particularly important because the Upper Sacramento River is not just a waterway passing through the region; it is also an important watershed and wildlife habitat. During the earlier stages of the response, crews used oil-absorbing materials near known seepage points to capture oil before it could spread. They also placed oil-retention booms in the fast-flowing river and removed contaminated gravel and stones from sections of the riverbed, replacing them with absorbent materials. These measures were intended to limit the movement of oil downstream and reduce further exposure to the surrounding environment.However, cleaning up an ecosystem is not as simple as removing the visible signs of pollution. The river and its banks need to be monitored to understand whether contamination is still present and whether the restored habitat is holding up. During the 2024 work, authorities regularly checked the water for oil and turbidity, collecting measurements upstream, downstream and near the construction site. This was especially important because removing the old retaining wall and excavating contaminated soil could disturb sediment and release trapped oil into the water.Even after the major cleanup was completed in 2025, monitoring remained necessary. In October 2026, oil was once again observed seeping from the soil along a section of the restored shoreline. Response teams installed containment barriers and booms, while crews removed additional contaminated sand and gravel. The authorities reported that no oiled wildlife had been observed during this response.Pollution does not always announce itself. Sometimes, it remains buried beneath layers of soil, quietly affecting the environment for decades before anyone realises the scale of the damage. The story of the Dunsmuir railyard is a reminder that environmental damage can outlast the industries and activities that caused it. Removing 75,000 gallons of oil and 100,000 tons of contaminated soil was a significant step, but the fresh seepage reported in 2026 shows that the work is far from over. Nature may have the ability to recover, but that recovery requires more than a one-time cleanup. It demands sustained attention, accountability and the willingness to repair damage long after it has been caused.
Article Summary: In Dunsmuir, California, oil from an old locomotive-fuelling facility had been leaking into the surrounding soil and the Sacramento River for decades. The contamination could be traced back to the early 1900s, when leaking tanks and equipment were used to fuel locomotives at the railyard. Removing 75,000 gallons of oil and 100,000 tons of contaminated soil was a significant step, but the fresh seepage reported in 2026 shows that the ability to recover is far from over.

Article Title: Sariska lost all its tigers to poaching by 2005 and had to bring them back from Ranthambore in 2008; now tigress ST-26 has been filmed with her first two cubs, taking the reserve’s tiger count to 58
Article Text:
(Image Credit: Canva)

Sariska Tiger Reserve Gets 2 New Cubs

The sanctuary of wildlife

The tiger comeback story

(Image Credit: Canva)

Planning your Sariska adventure

How to reach:

By Air:

By Train

By Road:

While hunting was a prestigious sport for the royals of the older times, their enjoyment cost the ecosystem and its inhabitants in irreversible ways. However, fortunately, the modern world became more conscious about nature and started looking at preserving the balance in natural habitats. This consciousness has provided us with incredible conservation stories, especially in India where landscapes are full of varied wildlife, from sensitive Himalayan species to an abundance in the Western Ghats. One such conservation success story comes from regal Rajasthan for the conservation of India's national pride, the Tiger.Welcome to Sariska Tiger Reserve, located roughly 200 km from Delhi, it is a wildlife escape in Rajasthan’s Alwar district. The tiger reserve became the site for the World’s First Tiger Relocation program in 2008 and is today studied as a successful case study. The strategy's success was declared in 2012 itself when tigress ST2 gave birth to 2 cubs. Now, the tiger population has reached 58 with ST-26 being filmed with her two newborn cubs last month. The moment feels like completing a full cycle as the 6-7 year old tigress was herself born in Sariska.Sariska used to serve as the hunting ground for the princely state of Alwar. The very first mention of the region goes way back to the Prahlad-Hiranyakashap story, and the Pandavas’ year-long exile in secrecy in Mahabharat (Virat Nagar). The region eventually gained prominence when it came under the control of the Bargujar Kings, who were part of the huge Gujara Pratihara empire in northern India.After independence, conservation efforts began with it being notified as a Wildlife Reserve in 1955. Its status was raised in 1958 with recognition as a Wildlife Sanctuary. Finally, it came under Project Tiger in 1979 and became Sariska Tiger Reserve. The landscape at the reserve is unlike other forests, it is dry the majority of the year. During summer, temperatures can even reach 45°C as the jungle turns ash brown due to heat. However , the monsoon season brings some relief to the region.By 2005, tigers had disappeared from the reserve. Their local extinction was a devastating setback, raising difficult questions about wildlife protection and the future of the landscape. Yet the story did not end there.In 2008, a pioneering programme began reintroducing tigers from Ranthambore to Sariska. The effort involved scientific planning, monitoring and continued protection, marking an important experiment in restoring a species to a landscape where it had vanished. According to a June 2026 announcement by India’s Press Information Bureau , Sariska had recovered to support 56 tigers, 18 years after the reintroduction programme began. The initiative is recognised as a landmark in wildlife conservation and a source of lessons for future tiger-recovery efforts. This number increased to 58 with two new cubs observed last month.This turned out to be the world’s first successful tiger relocation project, made possible by intricate planning, habitat protection, wildlife monitoring and local community efforts. A visit to Sariska becomes more meaningful when you see it not merely as a place to photograph a tiger, but as a landscape still working to protect its wildlife.The best way to explore the reserve is on an authorised jeep or canter safari. Winter, broadly from October to March, is a comfortable period for exploring the region, although mornings can be chilly. Summer can be hot, but wildlife activity around water sources may make it appealing to some visitors. Safari availability and timings vary by season, and visitors should check current rules before travelling.Sariska lies in Alwar district, Rajasthan.Jaipur International Airport is the nearest airport to Sariska. It is located approximately 133 km away from the reserve. After you land, you can hire a taxi or catch a bus to reach the reserve.: Alwar Junction is the nearest railway station and around 35 km from Sariska. Enough trains are available from major cities, including Delhi, Jaipur and Mumbai. From the station, taxis and local buses will be available to take you to Sariska.Sariska enjoys good road connectivity with several cities and towns across Rajasthan and neighbouring states.If travelling from Delhi, take NH48 (Delhi-Jaipur Highway) and continue via the Alwar-Bhiwadi Bypass Road. From Jaipur, follow NH48 and then take the Alwar-Jaipur Road towards the reserve.
Article Summary: Sariska Tiger Reserve is a wildlife sanctuary in Rajasthan's Alwar district. The reserve was the site for the World’s First Tiger Relocation program in 2008. The strategy's success was declared in 2012 itself when tigress ST2 gave birth to 2 cubs. Now, the tiger population has reached 58 with ST-26 being filmed with her two newborn cubs last month.

Article Title: Frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest crashed between 1979 and 1982 and no one knew why; nearly 50 years later, scientists tested over 370 preserved museum frogs and found a killer fungus that was absent
Article Text:
Brazilian Frog (Image Credit: Canva)

Who’s behind the decline?

(Image Credit: Canva)

Interesting patterns

The mystery behind the collapse of various civilisations has troubled scientists to this day. The fall of the Indus Valley Civilisation is still not certain, the most we have are multiple theories around it. Similar is the case with the tale behind evolution, decline and extinction of a few animal species that disappeared in mysterious circumstances within a very short period. The curiosity around these organisms have led the scientists to keep studying their lives even today. The discovery of new species in the current times indicate how nature has a way to stay concealed from humans. One such 50-year-old mystery was unfolded by the scientists about frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest. The population of these frogs declined dramatically between 1979 and 1982 but until now, nobody knew why it happened.The scientists struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil’s Atlantic Forest which is actually one of the world’s richest regions for amphibian diversity. The findings published in Molecular Ecology have uncovered evidence that has linked these disappearances to a deadly fungal disease.The study was conducted by researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU).Long after the frogs started to decline, a fungus believed to have originated in Asia was formally identified and described in 1999. This microscopic fungus named Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis caused the disease chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, which is said to be the cause behind the declining frog populations. The pathogen spread in the world during the 1970s and 1980s which led to the beginning of extinction of hundreds of amphibian species around the world. The absence of knowledge about the existence of the pathogen and its late discovery led to difficulty in determining whether it was responsible for these events.Before the discovery of the fungus, some researchers suggested that environmental factors such as climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the declines.Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research told the Science Direct that “While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances."The sample for the research were the preserved frogs housed in The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History. These preserved specimens offered an opportunity to examine the conditions before and after the disappearance events. It helped them track the arrival and spread of the fungus in the forest. More than 370 preserved frogs from 17 species were analysed during the study which aimed to search for spread of chytrid infection and the frequency of its spread.The blame was not easily implied to the pathogen when interesting patterns emerged after research. It was revealed that chytrid infection was not observed in specimens collected before 1979. However, in samples from the 1980s more than half tested positive for the fungus. The intriguing fact was that the species which showed the presence of the fungus were the ones whose populations did not decline drastically. Rather, the ones which did not show detectable signs of infection were the ones that suffered the most severe declines.This contradiction is explained by the scientists by concluding that the frogs that were naturally capable of tolerating the infection were able to survive even when the fungus attacked. While others that were more vulnerable could not adapt and hence, few or no infected individuals could ever be collected. Thus, due to the absence of exposure to the fungus and the disease before, chytrid spread rapidly bringing devastating effects for the amphibian species.The latest surveys at Brazil’s Boracéia Biological Station offer a rare glimmer of hope for amphibians. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers from the University of São Paulo revisited the site six times to compare its present-day frog population with historical museum records. Of the 17 species documented in the collection, 12 were found during the new surveys, while the remaining five could not be located. The results suggest that most local amphibian populations have recovered from the devastating declines of the early 1980s, when the chytrid fungus swept through the region. Interestingly, the fungus is still present, but some frog species may have gradually developed greater tolerance to the infection, allowing them to survive despite continued exposure.However, the findings of this discovery are being cautioned to be applied to this particular location. A generalisation of the results is not advisable and cannot automatically explain other disappearances of amphibian populations. Scientists are continuing the investigation into understanding the specifics around the discovery. Researchers are now examining DNA from preserved museum specimens to understand why certain species were more vulnerable while others managed to survive.
Article Summary: Scientists at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and Pennsylvania State University studied frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest. The population of these frogs declined dramatically between 1979 and 1982 but until now, nobody knew why it happened. A fungus believed to have originated in Asia was formally identified and described in 1999. This microscopic fungus caused the disease chytridiomycosis which is said to be the cause behind the declining frog populations. Researchers are now examining DNA from preserved museum specimens to understand why certain species were more vulnerable while others managed to survive.

Article Title: Six journalists killed, 33 years of defiance: Russia's last major independent newspaper shuts down
Article Text:
Ivan Zhilin, journalist of Novaya Gazeta, puts poster with sign 'Novaya Gazeta lived here' to cover the outlet's plaque on the office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a campaign by authorities

Crackdown on independent media

Russia's last major independent newspaper critical of the Kremlin, Novaya Gazeta, shut down its Moscow office on Monday after three decades, citing sustained pressure from government officials and security agencies.The newspaper, which has faced mounting restrictions since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, said authorities had forced its editorial team to cease operations.In a statement published on October 30, the newspaper said Russian authorities and security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations.”“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime,” the newspaper said, "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot.”On Monday, journalists cleared the Moscow office, slowly taking down portraits of six colleagues who were killed for their work. The photographs had hung in the newsroom where reporters and editors once planned their investigations.As staff gathered outside the building, a new sign was placed above the newspaper's former nameplate. It read, “Here lived Novaya Gazeta.”Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the newspaper to shut down almost every day over the past four-and-a-half years.“It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office -- this is our home, and we're losing it,” she said.Sergei Sokolov, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, expressed hope that it would eventually return.“We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues.”Founded in 1993, Novaya Gazeta earned a reputation for investigative journalism, particularly its reporting on human rights violations and corruption in Russia. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War.Politkovskaya was shot dead in her apartment building in 2006, during Vladimir Putin's first term as president.The newspaper faced increasing government pressure as the Kremlin tightened its grip on critics. The crackdown intensified after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, forcing several independent media organisations to close or move their operations abroad.Novaya Gazeta was fined over allegations that it had discredited Russia's armed forces. Authorities also designated it a “foreign agent”, a label that carries strong negative connotations and exposes those named to additional government scrutiny.Its online platforms were blocked, its printing house was seized, its media registration was revoked and its reader donation system was shut down. The latest order to vacate its Moscow office marked another blow to the publication.Longtime editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, also faced intimidation. In 2022, an attacker poured red paint over him on a train, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being designated a “foreign agent”.Some of the newspaper's journalists left Russia in 2022 and established a separate publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe. The outlet continues to criticise the Kremlin and its military campaign in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last major independent newspaper, shut down its Moscow office on Monday after three decades. The newspaper, which has faced mounting restrictions since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, said authorities had forced its editorial team to cease operations.

Article Title: Richard Simmons' Los Angeles home sells for $3.8 million after decades of ownership; inside the fitness icon's unusual residence with a key-shaped swimming pool
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Richard Simmons’ estate finally finds a buyer after months of price cuts and a bold relaunch

Image: Wikipedia

Agents repositioned the home as a development opportunity, valuing the land over the house itself

Staircase cherubs, patterned wallpaper and curved French doors gave the home its joyful personality

Disguises and quiet drives; how Richard Simmons lived behind closed doors in his final years

Richard Simmons’ Los Angeles home has sold for $3.8 million, ending a long chapter for the hilltop estate where the fitness icon lived for more than four decades. Set high above the Sunset Strip, the gated property offers panoramic city views, terraced gardens, an attic gym and a key-shaped pool. Simmons bought the four-bedroom residence in the 1980s and filled it with eccentric decoration that mirrored his vibrant public persona. He died there in July 2024, and the house has since passed through a sales campaign, several price cuts and a change in marketing approach before finding its new owner.According to Market Watch, the house first reached the market at $6.99 million in June 2025, 11 months after Simmons died. Its price was cut several times, with the latest reduction in May leaving it at $5.8 million. In April, the home made a return to the market with what listing agents Rachelle Rosten and Kelly deLaat of Douglas Elliman called a “highly strategic” sales approach, designed to maximise how buyers viewed its potential. The final price is roughly $3.2 million below where the listing began, and the sale completed more than two years after Simmons’ death.The new strategy followed what Rosten told Realtor was a careful reassessment of the property’s full potential. She said it was never meant to erase Simmons’ legacy, but to give it new life, and that the true value lies in the land rather than the existing house.The reasoning was practical. The current home occupies only a small portion of the 0.56-acre parcel, which rises in several usable tiers, with flat pads, terraced gardens and a dedicated pool level. That left room for a much larger modern mansion, whether built out from the existing structure or from scratch.Rosten acknowledged that the property’s celebrity provenance and distinctive design details would generate significant interest, though she suggested these were unlikely to be what clinched a sale. She pointed to the staircase cherubs, vibrant patterned wallpaper and curved French patio doors as touches that make the house both memorable and visually striking.Many people close to Simmons described the home as a deeply personal sanctuary. Spanning nearly 5,000 square feet, with four and a half bathrooms, it reflects a man who built an empire encouraging millions to exercise through his hugely successful “Sweatin’ to the Oldies” workout videos.The house drew fresh attention in May, when broadcast journalist Diane Sawyer visited to spend time with Simmons’ brother, Lenny Simmons, and his housekeeper, Teresa Reveles, for a special that aired on 12 May.Reveles told Sawyer that Simmons gradually withdrew from public life and ventured out only when he was sure nobody would recognise him. She said he often disguised himself in elaborate costumes, from clown outfits to women’s clothing, and that she would then drive him around the city so he could see its new buildings and shops.Reveles also described the days before his death. He had fallen the night before he died but was reluctant to seek medical attention, telling those around him that he simply wanted to stay at home. His final evening, she recalled, was spent watching television, eating dinner and speaking of his gratitude for his life and his supporters before going to bed.“The perfect buyer found this home,” Rosten told Realtor. Drawn to its rich history, heritage and pedigree, she said, the buyer plans to restore it to its classic roots. That is a notably different path from the redevelopment the listing had invited. Paul Czako of Gussman Czako Estates represented the buyer.
Article Summary: Richard Simmons’ Los Angeles home has sold for $3.8 million. The four-bedroom property offers panoramic city views, terraced gardens, an attic gym and a key- shaped pool. Simmons bought the home in the 1980s and filled it with eccentric decoration that mirrored his vibrant public persona.

Article Title: Mystery threat puts US bases in Britain on high alert, aircraft shifted
Article Text:
Unexpected aircraft movements from Mildenhall

Drone threat raises fresh concerns over US bases

A sudden security escalation at two major US military bases in Britain has triggered questions over a possible threat to American forces in Europe. US authorities have raised the alert level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to the second-highest security category, while several military aircraft have unexpectedly moved out of Mildenhall.According to a report by The War Zone (TWZ), the US military confirmed enhanced force protection measures at the two installations on November 9 but did not disclose what prompted the decision.A subsequent Wall Street Journal report, said both bases had been placed under Force Protection Condition Charlie (FPCON Charlie), a level activated when intelligence indicates terrorist activity is likely.The development comes amid renewed concerns over Iran-linked threats against American military installations overseas, following a security incident near another US-operated airbase in Britain earlier this year.In September 2026, British authorities arrested five men near RAF Fairford after three vans were found in the vicinity of the military installation. Although no explosives were discovered, the investigation subsequently led to two further arrests. One suspect was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service believed by British police to be Iran.The incident raised concerns about possible Iranian intelligence operations targeting US military assets in Britain.Tehran has denied involvement in the alleged plot.RAF Fairford had previously been used by American B-1B Lancer strategic bombers during military operations against Iran. The US subsequently withdrew the bombers from the installation amid concerns about potential threats.The latest security escalation coincided with unusual movements of American military aircraft from RAF Mildenhall.Flight-tracking observers reported that several KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refuelling aircraft were moved to other European locations, including Germany, Spain and Scotland. CV-22B Osprey special operations aircraft were also relocated from Mildenhall to RAF Lakenheath.According to subsequent reporting by Sky News, nine KC-135 tankers and three Ospreys were involved in the movements.The US Air Force said aircraft routinely move between installations for operational requirements and training. However, it did not establish whether these particular relocations were directly connected to the heightened security alert.RAF Mildenhall is a major American military hub in Britain. It hosts KC-135 Stratotankers, which extend the operational range of US fighter jets and bombers through aerial refuelling. The installation also houses RC-135 Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft, which collect intelligence and monitor military activity, alongside special operations aircraft.RAF Lakenheath, meanwhile, hosts F-15E Strike Eagle fighter-bombers and F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters. It is one of the most important US fighter installations in Europe and provides Washington with significant combat air capabilities in the region.The latest security alert has also drawn attention to the possibility of unmanned aerial systems being used to surveil or threaten American military installations in Britain. The concern is not without precedent.In November 2024, unidentified drones were repeatedly spotted flying near and over four UK airbases hosting US forces, including RAF Lakenheath, RAF Mildenhall, RAF Feltwell and RAF Fairford.The issue remains relevant because small drones can potentially be used to monitor aircraft movements, map security arrangements and gather intelligence around sensitive military infrastructure. Depending on their capabilities and payloads, they can also pose risks to flight operations and personnel.The possibility of such activity has resurfaced after RAF Lakenheath issued a public warning on November 9, urging residents to report suspicious activity, including unauthorised drone operations, around the installation.
Article Summary: US authorities have raised the alert level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to the second-highest security category. Several military aircraft have unexpectedly moved out of Mildenhal. Comes amid renewed concerns over Iran- linked threats against American military installations overseas.

Article Title: Who is Ahmed Moor? Gaza-born Palestinian-American writer takes on John Fetterman in 2028 Pennsylvania Senate race
Article Text:
Ahmed Moor

Who is Ahmed Moor?

What does Moor stand for?

Why is he challenging John Fetterman?

Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian-American writer and journalist born in Gaza, has entered the race for the US Senate in Pennsylvania, announcing a Democratic primary challenge to incumbent John Fetterman for the 2028 election.Aged 42, Moor is campaigning for free healthcare, childcare, affordable housing and stronger civil liberties. He also supports ending US military aid to Israel, putting him at odds with Fetterman's pro-Israel stance.Moor has said his campaign is not simply an attempt to unseat the Pennsylvania senator. Speaking to The Philadelphia Inquirer, he described his motivation as a broader effort to change how the government works.“I'm not really running against Fetterman. I'm running for good government. I'm running for the rule of law. I'm running because I believe in America,” he told the newspaper.Moor was born in Rafah, a city in southern Gaza, and is a Palestinian-American writer and journalist. He has spoken publicly about his Palestinian background and his views on US policy towards Israel.His political positions include withdrawing American aid from Israel and imposing sanctions to secure equal rights for Palestinians.These proposals place him on a different footing from Fetterman, who has consistently defended Israel's military campaign in Gaza following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.Moor has described his programme as a “dignity agenda”, with proposals including free healthcare, free childcare and affordable housing.In a post on X announcing his Senate bid, he also identified ending the war in Iran as a campaign priority. He called for accountability over what he described as genocide, the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and corruption. Protecting civil liberties in the US was another commitment he outlined.His criticism extends beyond Republican policies. Moor has expressed little confidence in the Democratic Party's current leadership, arguing that it needs to respond more effectively to the country's political and constitutional challenges.He has also backed stronger restrictions on corporate and special-interest influence in government, making political accountability a central part of his campaign message.Moor's candidacy comes as Fetterman faces criticism from Democrats over his voting record and support for Republicans on several issues, particularly Israel.Fetterman entered the Senate in 2023 after campaigning as a progressive outsider. However, his positions have since disappointed some Democrats who supported his 2022 campaign. He has also received praise from President Donald Trump, who has described him as “a great guy” and said he would welcome him into the Republican Party.The senator has said he has no intention of leaving the Democrats, but warned last year that he would reconsider if the party formally adopted an anti-Israel position.Moor's campaign presents a direct policy contrast, particularly over US support for Israel. However, he has framed his candidacy around a wider set of domestic and foreign policy priorities rather than solely as a challenge to the incumbent.
Article Summary: Ahmed Moor, 42, is a Palestinian-American writer and journalist. He has announced a Democratic primary challenge to incumbent John Fetterman. Moor is campaigning for free healthcare, childcare, affordable housing and stronger civil liberties. He also supports ending US military aid to Israel.

Article Title: A federal judge halted Trump's border wall work across Texas's 500-mile Big Bend sector; 38 days later, the Supreme Court cleared construction to resume while the lawsuit continues
Article Text:
Why did a judge halt construction?

What did the Supreme Court decide?

Why is the Big Bend region controversial?

A much larger border-wall ambition

US President Donald Trump has a penchant for dreaming up big projects, from his long-promised wall along the US-Mexico border to sweeping plans for reshaping federal buildings and public spaces. But one of his most ambitious border-security projects has run into a legal battle over its impact on one of America's most striking natural landscapes. On November 9, the US Supreme Court cleared the way for his administration to resume construction in Texas's Big Bend region, just 38 days after a federal judge ordered work to stop over concerns that the government had exceeded its authority to bypass environmental laws, as per a report by CBS News.The ruling allows construction of border barriers and related infrastructure across the Big Bend sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the US-Mexico border and includes Big Bend National Park. The Supreme Court's decision temporarily pauses a lower court's injunction while the legal challenge continues. It does not settle the underlying dispute over whether the administration can lawfully proceed with the project.The case has become a major test of how far the federal government can go in using its authority to accelerate border construction, particularly in environmentally sensitive areas.The dispute began after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced plans in February 2026 to expand border barriers and roads through the Big Bend region. Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem issued waivers allowing construction to bypass several federal environmental and historic-preservation requirements. Her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued additional waivers. The administration invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the DHS secretary authority to waive legal requirements considered necessary to ensure the rapid construction of border barriers and roads near the southern border.The project includes 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls in certain areas, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and surveillance infrastructure. Government filings described plans for barriers and roads extending more than 300 miles in the region, although the wider Big Bend Border Patrol sector covers approximately 517 miles.Environmental groups, a local river guide and a religious organisation challenged the waivers in court in April. They argued that the administration had used a law intended to address areas of high illegal entry to justify construction in a region that records some of the lowest migrant apprehension numbers along the US-Mexico border.On October 2, US District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction, stopping construction and other ground-disturbing activities across the Big Bend sector. In her subsequent written opinion, she found that the challengers were likely to establish that the administration had exceeded its authority when issuing the waivers. The judge also questioned the government's description of Big Bend as an area of high illegal entry. The plaintiffs pointed out that the sector accounts for a relatively small share of apprehensions despite covering a substantial portion of the border.The Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower court's order was obstructing its ability to secure the border and combat drug trafficking and illegal crossings. On November 9, the justices granted the administration's emergency request and temporarily lifted the injunction. The unsigned decision said the lower court's order was delaying construction and impeding the government's ability to advance its interests in border security. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter, saying she would have rejected the administration's request for emergency relief.The ruling is an interim victory for Trump, but it does not mean the environmental groups have lost their lawsuit. The legal challenge will continue, and the Supreme Court's decision allows construction to proceed while the broader questions are considered.The administration has argued that more than 89,000 people attempting to cross into the US illegally were apprehended in the Big Bend sector between 2021 and 2025. It has also cited drug seizures and the activities of criminal cartels in neighbouring parts of Mexico, warning that leaving gaps in border protection could encourage trafficking and illegal entry. The challengers, however, maintain that the region's rugged terrain already makes illegal crossings difficult and that the scale of the proposed construction is unnecessary.The proposed project has drawn attention because of the landscape it could alter. Big Bend is known for its desert ecosystems, dramatic canyons, mountains and the Rio Grande, which forms part of the US-Mexico boundary. The wider area includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and sections of the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River corridor.Environmental groups and local residents argue that construction could fragment wildlife habitats, damage historic and cultural sites, disturb vegetation and affect access to the river. They have also raised concerns about the consequences for tourism, ranching and businesses that depend on the region's natural landscape. The opposition has extended beyond environmental organisations. Local landowners, cattle ranchers, river guides and politicians from both parties have questioned whether a large physical barrier is necessary in an area with relatively low migrant apprehension numbers.The administration, meanwhile, says it is not planning to construct a continuous 30-foot pedestrian wall through Big Bend National Park itself. Customs and Border Protection has said the park would instead see patrol roads, surveillance equipment and approximately 17 miles of vehicle barriers. The broader project also involves construction on private and public land outside the park.The Big Bend project is part of Trump's wider effort to expand physical barriers along the southern border, a promise that has been central to his immigration agenda for more than a decade. Congress allocated approximately $46 billion for border-wall projects, allowing the administration to accelerate construction across several sections of the frontier. The Big Bend portion has been particularly contentious because of its ecological and cultural significance. According to reporting by The Washington Post, the project in the region has been estimated at around $1.7 billion.Construction activity had already begun in parts of the area before the legal intervention. Images of bulldozers clearing land near Big Bend National Park triggered criticism from environmentalists and lawmakers, prompting officials to announce a temporary pause on work inside the park.With the Supreme Court now allowing construction to resume, the administration can move ahead while the lawsuit remains unresolved. For conservationists and local communities, however, the concern is that damage to the desert, river corridor and wildlife habitats could be difficult to reverse even if the courts eventually rule against the project.
Article Summary: The US Supreme Court cleared the way for his administration to resume construction in Texas's Big Bend region, just 38 days after a federal judge ordered work to stop. The ruling allows construction of border barriers and related infrastructure across the Big Bend sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the US-Mexico border. The Supreme Court's decision temporarily pauses a lower court's injunction while the legal challenge continues.

Article Title: In 2023, Washington fined a cattle-ranching couple $267,540 over wetlands they say were stockwater ponds; three years later, they are still fighting restoration demands they estimate could exceed $3.7
Article Text:
Photo: Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation

What Ecology says happened

The Kings’ response

Photo: Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation

The fight over a jury trial

The cost of restoration

Why the case matters

A Washington cattle-ranching couple has spent three years fighting a $267,540 state penalty and restoration orders they say could cost more than $3.7 million. Wade and Teresa King, who operate King Ranch in Grant and Douglas counties, argue that the sites are longstanding stockwater ponds for their livestock, while the Washington State Department of Ecology says they damaged naturally occurring wetlands, including rare alkali wetlands.The dispute began in February 2023, when Ecology fined the Kings and ordered restoration work near Park Lake in Grant County. In January 2025, the agency issued a second order involving 11 additional wetlands in neighboring Douglas County, bringing the total number of affected sites to 34.Ecology’s investigation found that the Kings excavated, recontoured and placed fill in 6.37 acres of naturally occurring wetlands in Grant County. The department says it relied on site visits, soil and water analysis, satellite imagery and aerial photographs dating back to 1949.According to Ecology, the aerial and satellite images showed the wetlands undisturbed until 2021, when the excavation occurred. The agency says many of the sites are rare alkali wetlands, which form in arid eastern Washington when mineral-rich groundwater rises to the surface and mixes with runoff and snowmelt.Ecology says those wetlands can take centuries to form and often dry out during hot weather, leaving bright white salt crusts or playas. The department argues that those seasonal changes do not make the areas artificial ponds, and that the Kings’ actions damaged wetlands protected under Washington’s Water Pollution Control Act of 1945.The agency also says it found no evidence that the water bodies had ever been modified as stockwater ponds. It maintains that formal enforcement involving ranching is rare and that it has no record of previously penalizing a livestock operator solely for damaging wetlands.The Kings reject Ecology’s characterization of the sites. They say the ponds are longstanding stockwater ponds used to provide water for cattle, and that the agency is treating ordinary ranching infrastructure as protected wetlands.Teresa King has said the restoration orders would be financially devastating and practically impossible because the areas were never wetlands in the first place. She and Wade argue that they are being asked to turn non-wetlands into wetlands, a demand they see as both unachievable and unfair.The Kings also say Ecology has not provided enough detail about how they are supposed to comply with the restoration requirements. Wade King argues that the wetlands designation gives the department more authority over the land than it would have if the areas were recognized as stockwater ponds.For the family, the stakes extend beyond money. The Kings have ranched in Grant and Douglas counties since the 1950s, and Teresa says multiple generations now live and work on the property. She describes the fight as a defense of the livestock water rights relied on by ranchers across Washington.The Kings initially challenged the penalty and restoration orders through Washington’s Pollution Control Hearings Board, an administrative panel that does not offer jury trials. They later filed a separate lawsuit in Grant County Superior Court, arguing that they were entitled to a jury trial and that the administrative process violated that right.In March 2026, a judge dismissed that lawsuit, ruling that the Kings first had to complete the administrative process. The Kings appealed, and in September 2026 the Washington Court of Appeals granted a temporary stay of the Pollution Control Hearings Board proceedings while the appeal continues.Wade King has criticized the administrative process, saying it places too much power in the executive branch and rarely favors property owners. Ecology, meanwhile, says the Kings appealed both the 2023 penalty and the 2025 administrative order, and that the board later required them to grant access to sites they had previously denied inspectors.Oliver Dunford, a senior attorney with the Pacific Legal Foundation representing the Kings, has said they are prepared to take the case to the U.S. Supreme Court if necessary. He argues that the Seventh Amendment should apply against the states and that the Kings should have had a jury trial.The Kings’ attorneys estimate that complying with Ecology’s orders could cost more than $3.7 million. That figure is far higher than the original $267,540 penalty and illustrates why the dispute has become so consequential for the family.Ecology says it issued the penalty after repeated attempts to resolve the concerns without formal enforcement. It says the Kings refused to cooperate with those efforts, while the Kings maintain that they have always cared for the land and water their livelihood depends on.The agency says wetlands provide flood and erosion control, recharge groundwater, improve water quality and support plant and animal habitat. It also notes that livestock operators who want to build stock ponds or divert surface water may need local and state permits, water rights or other authorization.The King Ranch case has become more than a local land-use dispute. It raises questions about how states balance environmental protection with agricultural operations, and whether property owners facing large penalties should have access to a jury trial.For the Kings, the outcome could determine whether they can continue operating a multigenerational ranch without a restoration bill they believe is impossible to pay. For Ecology, the case is about enforcing protections for wetlands it says were damaged through unauthorized excavation.The case remains unresolved. The Court of Appeals has paused the administrative proceedings while it considers the jury-trial issue, and both sides continue to present sharply different accounts of what the land was before the excavation began.
Article Summary: Wade and Teresa King argue that the sites are longstanding stockwater ponds for their livestock. The Washington State Department of Ecology says they damaged naturally occurring wetlands. The dispute began in February 2023, when Ecology fined the Kings and ordered restoration work.

Article Title: Troy Lotspeich’s great-grandfather bought their ranch in northern Oklahoma in 1903; today the family rotates 600 cow-calf pairs through 25 paddocks on 10,000 acres of native grass, winning landowner o
Article Text:
How 25 paddocks help protect the grassland

A prairie ecosystem shared with wildlife

A family legacy that has changed with the land

A ranch in northwestern Oklahoma has remained in one family for more than a century, but its latest distinction comes from how the land is being managed. Troy Lotspeich’s great-grandfather bought the family's current ranch in 1903. Today, the 10,000-acre property is home to 600 cattle that are moved through 25 grazing paddocks, giving native grasslands time to recover while supporting a diverse population of wildlife. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (ODWC) has now named the Lotspeich family its 2026 Landowner Conservationist of the Year.The award, announced on October 12, recognises the family's efforts to balance cattle production with wildlife habitat conservation. According to the department, the main Lotspeich Ranch in northern Harper County comprises native grasses, forbs and shrubs. The family also owns an additional 3,950 acres of farmland in Beaver County, including 750 acres of irrigated land.The ranch's history stretches back to the 1890s, when Lotspeich's great-grandfather first arrived in Oklahoma and purchased a quarter-section of land. He subsequently bought the property that became the family's current ranch in 1903.Generations later, the land continues to support a working cattle operation, but its management has increasingly focused on maintaining the prairie ecosystem.The family follows a rotational grazing system in which its 600 cattle are moved through 25 paddocks across the 10,000-acre ranch during the growing season. Instead of allowing livestock to graze continuously across the same stretch of land, the approach concentrates grazing in one area for a shorter period before cattle are moved elsewhere. The system follows a principle known as "take half, leave half", which means leaving enough grass behind for vegetation to recover and continue providing food and shelter for wildlife. The department describes the approach as high-intensity, low-duration grazing. It can improve soil conditions and organic matter, helping the ground absorb and retain more rainwater.Water availability is particularly important in this part of Oklahoma. The region receives an average of only around 22 inches of precipitation annually, making it essential to conserve moisture and allow native vegetation to recover between grazing periods. To make the system work across the property, the family has installed approximately 35 miles of water lines connected to 20 stock tanks. These provide at least one water source for each paddock, reducing the need for cattle to travel long distances to drink. Troy also monitors grazing pressure through structures called grazing exclosures, which allow him to compare vegetation in protected areas with grass exposed to livestock.During winter, the cattle are moved away from the native grassland and onto the family's crop ground. There, they graze on wheat pasture supplemented with alfalfa hay or grain produced on the irrigated farmland.The ranch's conservation work has helped sustain a range of wildlife species, including northern bobwhite quail, white-tailed deer, mule deer, elk, prairie dogs, burrowing owls, ring-necked pheasants and wild turkeys. Ducks, geese and sandhill cranes also use the property's ponds and river.Native grasses and forbs play an important role in maintaining this habitat. They provide food and cover for wildlife, while healthy vegetation helps protect soil and retain rainfall. Allowing grasslands time to recover after grazing also helps maintain the varied plant growth that supports different species. Fire is another part of the landscape's natural history. According to ODWC, wildfires have helped shape the vegetation on the ranch. Native prairie plants are adapted to fire and can continue growing even when rainfall is limited. Fire also helps maintain an ecosystem that historically evolved with periodic burning.The family also allows guided hunts for northern bobwhite and white-tailed deer, while youth hunts are organised on the ranch. The Lotspeiches raise and train their own bird dogs, maintaining a connection between the family's ranching traditions and outdoor activities.The family's relationship with wildlife has evolved over generations. An account from a 1965 edition of Oklahoma Wildlife magazine quoted Troy's grandfather, Kenny Lotspeich, recalling that the ranch once displayed "no hunting" signs. He later decided to remove them, explaining that the signs were keeping genuine friends away while failing to stop poachers from taking birds.Today, the family works closely with the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, the Natural Resources Conservation Service and the Farm Service Agency. Troy is also associated with conservation organisations including Pheasants Forever/Quail Forever and the National Wild Turkey Federation. He participates in a Candidate Conservation Agreement with Assurances programme for lesser prairie-chickens, a species whose grassland habitat has faced pressure across parts of the Great Plains.The family's recognition also highlights the importance of private landowners in wildlife conservation in Oklahoma. More than 95% of the state is privately owned, according to the wildlife department, making cooperation with farmers and ranchers important for protecting habitats beyond public conservation areas.
Article Summary: Troy Lotspeich’s great-grandfather bought the family's current ranch in 1903. Today, the 10,000-acre property is home to 600 cattle that are moved through 25 grazing paddocks, giving native grasslands time to recover. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (ODWC) has now named the Lotspeiches its 2026 Landowner Conservationist of the Year.

Article Title: A fake GoFundMe collected $17,750 after 67 people died in a Washington plane crash; a Russian lawyer spotted suspicious emails and helped get the campaign removed
Article Text:
Representative image

Fake fundraiser claimed to support family of Kansas farmers

Russian lawyer noticed suspicious details in email exchange

Alleged $15,000 payment request raised further concerns

GoFundMe removes campaign and refunds donors

GoFundMe directs donors to verified crash-related fundraisers

A fraudulent GoFundMe campaign claiming to raise money for the family of two victims of the January 2025 Washington plane crash collected $17,750 before being taken down, after a Russian lawyer identified suspicious activity and alerted the fundraising platform. The campaign, which had a target of $150,000, claimed to support the family of Kansas farmers Bob and Lori Schrock, who were among the 67 people killed when an American Eagle passenger aircraft collided with a US Army helicopter near Washington, DC. Gauthier Daniel Igorevich, a Moscow-based criminal lawyer, became suspicious after contacting the person listed as the fundraiser's representative. His investigation revealed unusual email exchanges, including a request for a $15,000 transfer to a Skrill account.The GoFundMe campaign appeared after the January 29, 2025, collision involving American Eagle Flight 5342 and a US Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. All 64 people aboard the passenger aircraft and all three helicopter crew members died.Among the victims were Bob and Lori Schrock, a farming couple from Kiowa, Kansas. They operated a canola and wheat farming business and were travelling from Wichita to Washington when the collision occurred.The fundraiser claimed to collect donations for the Schrock family and set a target of $150,000. It listed a contact named "Sam Lorri Otim", supposedly from Kiowa, Kansas. However, when DTN investigated the campaign, it could not find anyone by that name living in the town, and the listed contact did not respond to the publication's enquiries.Gauthier Daniel Igorevich, a Moscow-based criminal lawyer with Trunov, Ayvar and Partners, came across the fundraiser while researching a potential legal case connected to the plane crash. He was representing families of Russian citizens who had died in the collision, including relatives of former Russian-born figure skating world champions Yevgenia Shishkova and Vadim Naumov.After finding the campaign, Igorevich contacted the listed representative to offer legal assistance to the Schrock family. However, the responses raised concerns. The person communicating with him did not provide a name and referred to themselves only as a "family representative".Igorevich also found that the photographs used on the fundraising page were publicly available.
